text: # Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato (Cornell CALS)

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text: ## Diagnostic Symptomology

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text: Bacterial spot of tomato is caused by several species of *Xanthomonas*, predominantly *Xanthomonas perforans* and *Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria*. Foliar symptoms begin as small, water-soaked, circular to irregular lesions (less than 1/8 inch or 3 mm in diameter) on leaves. As lesions age, they turn dark brown to black and often develop a greasy appearance. Lesions may coalesce, causing extensive foliar blighting, yellowing (chlorosis), and premature leaf drop

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text: . On green fruit, spots begin as small, slightly raised black blisters that enlarge up to 1/4 inch, becoming brown, scabby, rough, and sunken with irregular margins.

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text:
## Environmental Epidemiology
The bacteria survive on contaminated seed, volunteer tomato plants, and infected solanaceous crop debris. Infection and rapid disease spread are strongly favored by warm temperatures between 75°F and 86°F (24°C to 30°C) combined with high relative humidity, frequent rainfall, or overhead sprinkler irrigation. Bacteria enter through natural leaf openings (stomata) or physical wounds caused by wind, sandblasting, pruning, or insect feeding.

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text:
## Cultural Management Practices
1. **Certified Disease-Free Seed:** Use only certified pathogen-free seed. If seed source is uncertain, treat seed with hot water (122°F / 50°C for exactly 25 minutes) to eradicate internal and external bacterial contamination without damaging germination.
2. **Crop Rotation:** Implement a minimum 2-year crop rotation away from all solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, eggplants) to starve overwintering bacterial populations in the soil.

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text:
3. **Irrigation Management:** Avoid overhead irrigation. Use drip or trickle irrigation beneath plastic mulch to keep foliage dry.
4. **Sanitation:** Never work in tomato fields when foliage is wet from dew or rain, as bacteria are easily transferred on workers' hands, clothing, and machinery. Thoroughly sanitize wooden stakes and harvest bins using a 10% sodium hypochlorite solution or quaternary ammonium sanitizers.

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text:
## Chemical Control & Bactericide Strategy
Preventative bactericidal applications are essential because therapeutic cure of established bacterial infections is impossible:
- **Copper + Mancozeb Tank Mix:** Apply fixed copper bactericides (such as copper hydroxide or basic copper sulfate at 1.5 to 2.0 lb/acre) combined with an EBDC fungicide (such as mancozeb at 1.5 lb/acre). The combination releases more free copper ions, overcoming moderate levels of bacterial copper tolerance.

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text:
- **Plant Defense Activator:** Apply acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard 50WG at 0.33 to 0.75 oz/acre) to induce systemic acquired resistance (SAR). Begin Actigard applications preventatively after transplanting when plants are established, prior to disease onset.
- **Application Intervals:** Maintain a 7- to 10-day spray schedule under dry conditions, shortening intervals to 5 to 7 days during warm, rainy weather. Strictly observe label reentry intervals (REI) and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).

metadata.title: Bacterial Spot and Speck of Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
metadata.pathogen: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria

text:
# Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida (UF/IFAS Extension)

## Overview & Pathogen Biology
Bacterial spot caused by *Xanthomonas perforans* is the most economically damaging foliar disease of fresh-market tomato production in humid subtropical and tropical environments. The pathogen attacks all above-ground plant parts including leaves, stems, flowers, and fruit. Severe defoliation results in major yield loss and exposes developing tomato fruit to solar injury (sunscald).

metadata.title: Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida
metadata.institution: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-73)
metadata.authors: Gary E. Vallad, Pamela D. Roberts

text:
## Copper Resistance & Chemical Strategies
Widespread resistance to copper bactericides exists in field populations of *Xanthomonas perforans*:
1. **Copper plus Mancozeb Synergism:** Routine reliance on copper alone frequently fails due to copper-tolerant strains. The tank-mixture of fixed copper (copper hydroxide or copper octanoate) with mancozeb is critical to generate toxic levels of soluble copper ions that kill resistant bacteria.

metadata.title: Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida
metadata.institution: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-73)
metadata.authors: Gary E. Vallad, Pamela D. Roberts

text: 2. **Plant Host Defense Activators:** Acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard) induces systemic acquired resistance (SAR) in tomato plants. To optimize efficacy and avoid plant stunting, apply Actigard at recommended low doses (0.33 to 0.75 oz/acre) starting 7 to 10 days post-transplant, repeating every 7 to 10 days for up to six to eight applications per season.

metadata.title: Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida
metadata.institution: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-73)
metadata.authors: Gary E. Vallad, Pamela D. Roberts

text: 3. **Bacteriophage Formulations:** Bacteriophage bio-bactericides (AgriPhage) target specific strains of *Xanthomonas*. Apply bacteriophages in early morning or evening to minimize degradation by solar ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Do not tank-mix phages directly with concentrated copper compounds without testing compatibility.

metadata.title: Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida
metadata.institution: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-73)
metadata.authors: Gary E. Vallad, Pamela D. Roberts

text:
## Biological Control Options
- **Microbial Antagonists:** Formulations of *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* (strain D747) or *Bacillus subtilis* provide moderate suppression of bacterial spot when applied preventatively as protective foliage coatings. Biologicals are especially valuable in organic tomato production systems where synthetic bactericides are prohibited.

metadata.title: Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida
metadata.institution: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-73)
metadata.authors: Gary E. Vallad, Pamela D. Roberts

text:
## Post-Harvest Field Hygiene & Sanitation
- **Crop Residue Destruction:** Immediately disc, flail, or plow under tomato crop residues immediately following the final harvest. Rapid tissue decomposition degrades bacterial survival shelters in the soil.
- **Volunteer Control:** Actively eradicate volunteer tomato and pepper plants, as well as nightshade weed species (such as *Solanum americanum*), in field perimeters, ditch banks, and adjacent fallow fields between growing seasons.

metadata.title: Management of Bacterial Spot on Tomato in Florida
metadata.institution: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS PP-73)
metadata.authors: Gary E. Vallad, Pamela D. Roberts

text: # Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight (Purdue Extension)

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text: ## Symptomology & Identification

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text: Early blight is caused by the fungal pathogen *Alternaria solani*. Symptoms first emerge on the oldest, lowermost leaves as small, circular, brown to black spots. As spots expand to 1/4 to 1/2 inch in diameter, they develop distinctive concentric ridges resembling a target board or bullseye pattern. The tissue surrounding the lesion frequently becomes yellow (chlorotic). As lesions multiply, entire lower leaves turn brown, wither, and drop from the plant. This progressive defoliation works upward through the canopy, exposing fruit to sunscald

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text: . This progressive defoliation works upward through the canopy, exposing fruit to sunscald. On stems, dark, sunken, oval cankers may form (termed collar rot when occurring at the soil line on young transplants). On green or ripe fruit, lesions occur near the stem attachment (calyx end) as dark, leathery, sunken, concentric depressions.

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text:
## Overwintering & Disease Cycle
*Alternaria solani* overwinters in infested tomato vines, potato debris, and wild solanaceous weeds (such as black nightshade and horsenettle). Spores (conidia) are produced abundantly during warm, humid weather and are disseminated by wind currents, rain splash, and mechanical equipment. Infection occurs rapidly when leaf surfaces remain wet from dew or rain for 8 or more hours at temperatures between 75°F and 85°F (24°C to 29°C).

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text:
## Cultural Management Guidelines
1. **Crop Rotation:** Practice a strict 2- to 3-year crop rotation out of solanaceous crops. Do not plant tomatoes where tomatoes, potatoes, eggplants, or peppers grew in the previous two seasons.
2. **Plant Spacing & Trellising:** Space plants adequately (18 to 24 inches within rows, 5 to 6 feet between rows) and stake or cage plants to promote rapid drying of foliage after dew and rain.

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text:
3. **Mulching & Pruning:** Apply straw, plastic mulch, or landscape fabric to provide a physical barrier preventing rain from splashing soil-borne fungal spores onto lower leaves. Prune lower suckers and leaves up to 12 inches above the mulch line once the plant is established.
4. **Watering Practices:** Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses. Avoid overhead irrigation; if overhead watering is unavoidable, irrigate early in the morning so sun and wind dry the leaves within 2 hours.

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text:
## Fungicide Spray Programs
- **Preventative Protectants:** Begin applications early in the season before disease appears or when first fruit cluster reaches walnut size:
  - Chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik, Daconil at 1.5 to 2.0 pt/acre) or Mancozeb (Dithane, Manzate at 1.5 to 2.0 lb/acre) applied every 7 to 10 days.
- **Targeted Systemic Fungicides:** When disease pressure is high, alternate protectants with systemic fungicides:
  - Azoxystrobin (Quadris - FRAC 11), Boscalid (Endura - FRAC 7), or Difenoconazole / Cyprodinil (Inspire Super - FRAC 3/9).

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text:
- Always rotate FRAC codes to prevent the development of fungicide resistance.
- **Organic Protectants:** Fixed copper fungicides (copper hydroxide) or sulfur products provide fair suppression when applied frequently before infection.

metadata.title: Foliar Diseases of Tomato: Early Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, and Anthracnose
metadata.institution: Purdue University Extension (BP-85-W)

text: # Tomato: Early Blight Management (UC IPM Guidelines)

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text: ## Disease Overview & Field Symptoms

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text: Early blight is caused by the fungus *Alternaria solani*. Although called "early" blight, the disease frequently becomes severe later in the season as the tomato fruit load increases and nitrogen levels in the canopy begin to decline. Stressed or heavy-yielding vines are particularly susceptible. Leaf spots are leathery, brown, circular, and show dark concentric rings, resembling an archery target. Collar rot symptoms can girdle the stems of transplants. Fruit infections occur at the stem-end calyx attachment, forming a sunken black crater covered with dark velvety spores.

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text:
## Environmental Triggers & Epidemiology
- Optimum fungal growth occurs between 75°F and 85°F (24°C to 29°C).
- Prolonged wet periods (at least 6 to 8 hours of continuous leaf wetness from rain, sprinkler irrigation, or heavy coastal fog) are necessary for spore germination and host penetration.
- Spores survive for more than one year on buried plant residues and on alternative solanaceous hosts.

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text:
## Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Practices
1. **Resistant & Tolerant Cultivars:** When available, select tomato varieties with partial resistance or tolerance to *Alternaria solani* to slow down epidemic progress.
2. **Nutritional Balance:** Maintain adequate, balanced nitrogen fertilization throughout the growing season. Plants suffering nitrogen deficiency senesce prematurely and suffer accelerated early blight defoliation.

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text:
3. **Deep Plowing & Sanitation:** After harvest, deeply plow under crop residue to accelerate fungal decomposition by soil microorganisms. Eliminate volunteer solanaceous weeds around field borders.
4. **Avoid Overhead Irrigation:** In arid and semi-arid production zones, furrow or subsurface drip irrigation keeps the plant canopy dry and almost completely suppresses early blight development.

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text:
## Chemical Control Schedules
- Begin preventative fungicide applications when the first fruit cluster sets or when early blight symptoms are detected on lower leaves.
- **Protectant Treatments:** Chlorothalonil or mancozeb provide reliable preventative protection. Apply on a 7- to 14-day schedule depending on rainfall frequency.
- **Systemic Products:** When weather favors disease, incorporate translaminar and systemic materials such as pyraclostrobin (Cabrio - FRAC 11) or fluopyram + trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation - FRAC 7/11).

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text: - **Organic Options:** Certified organic formulations of copper hydroxide (Kocide 3000) or *Bacillus subtilis* (Serenade ASO) applied preventatively can slow early blight progress under moderate disease pressure.

metadata.title: Tomato: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)

text: # Late Blight Management in Tomato (Cornell CALS & USABlight)

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
## Diagnostic Features of Late Blight
Late blight is caused by the oomycete *Phytophthora infestans* (an organism related to brown algae rather than true fungi). It is an extremely destructive pathogen capable of completely destroying entire fields of tomato and potato crops within 7 to 10 days if left unmanaged.
- **Foliar Symptoms:** Initial lesions appear as pale green, water-soaked, irregular areas on leaves. Under humid conditions, lesions expand rapidly into large, purplish-brown to dark brown necrotic patches.

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
- **White Sporulation:** In damp, foggy, or rainy conditions (relative humidity > 90%), a characteristic white, delicate, cottony growth (sporangia and sporangiophores) forms on the undersides of infected leaves and along affected green stems.
- **Stem & Petiole Cankers:** Dark brown, greasy lesions frequently girdle petioles and green stems, causing rapid collapse of distal foliage.
- **Fruit Symptoms:** Green or ripe fruit develop large, firm, rough, dark brown to olive-colored greasy lesions that remain firm unless invaded by secondary bacterial soft rot organisms.

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
## Epidemiology & Weather Requirements
Unlike early blight and bacterial spot which prefer warm conditions, *Phytophthora infestans* thrives in cool, wet, humid weather:
- Ideal daytime temperatures: 60°F to 75°F (15°C to 24°C).
- Cool nighttime temperatures: 50°F to 60°F (10°C to 15°C) with fog, dew, or rain.
- Temperatures above 86°F (30°C) halt pathogen spore production and slow down lesion expansion.
- Millions of microscopic sporangia are produced per lesion and can be transported aloft by wind currents for 5 to 10 miles.

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
## Disease Forecasting & Scouting
- Monitor the national **USABlight** network and regional weather-based disease forecasting systems (such as BlightCast and NEWA).
- When weather conditions reach high-risk severity thresholds (accumulated Late Blight Disease Severity Values, DSVs), preventative fungicide coverage must be established immediately prior to rain events.

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
## Resistant Cultivars
Planting resistant tomato varieties offers durable genetic protection:
- Cultivars carrying both the *Ph-2* and *Ph-3* resistance genes (such as **Mountain Magic**, **Defiant PHR**, **Plum Regal**, and **Iron Lady**) exhibit exceptional resistance to the predominant USABlight clonal lineages (including US-23).

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
## Fungicide Recommendations
1. **Preventative Protectants:** Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper fungicides on a 5- to 7-day interval before late blight is reported in the region.
2. **Targeted Oomycete Systemics:** Once late blight is confirmed locally or weather is conducive, transition to targeted translaminar or systemic oomycete fungicides:
   - **Cymoxanil (Curzate 60DF):** Possesses 24- to 48-hour curative / post-infection kickback activity; must be tank-mixed with a protectant (chlorothalonil or mancozeb).

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text:
- **Mandipropamid (Revus):** High preventative and anti-sporulant efficacy.
   - **Fluopicolide (Presidio):** Systemic oomycide with excellent translaminar movement.
   - **Propamocarb (Previcur Flex):** Systemic protectant.
3. **Organic Production:** Fixed copper fungicides (such as Champ, Badge, or Cueva) provide preventative protection if leaf surfaces are completely coated prior to spore deposition. Copper has zero curative kickback activity once tissue is infected.

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text: 4. **Immediate Rogueing:** When an initial hot-spot plant is detected, bag the plant in plastic on a dry sunny midday, cut at the base, and remove from the field to extinguish the localized spore source.

metadata.title: Late Blight Management in Tomato
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension (Vegetable Program & USABlight)

text: # Tomato: Late Blight Management (UC IPM Guidelines)

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text: ## Symptoms and Field Diagnosis

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text: *Phytophthora infestans* infects leaves, stems, and fruit of tomato. Foliar lesions begin as pale green, water-soaked spots that rapidly enlarge into dark brown to black blighted areas. When leaves are examined in the morning during periods of high humidity or wetness, a fine white moldy growth composed of sporangiophores and sporangia is visible on the underside of the leaves at the margins of the necrotic lesions. Stems develop dark brown cankers that can cause the collapse of entire branches

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text: . Stems develop dark brown cankers that can cause the collapse of entire branches. Green tomato fruit develop dark, firm, greasy-looking, rough brown lesions with distinct borders, which do not soften unless invaded by secondary rots.

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text:
## Pathogen Survival & Overwintering Reservoirs
Unlike fungal pathogens that form dormant resting structures in dry crop residue, *Phytophthora infestans* requires living host tissue to survive from one season to the next:
- It overwinters primarily in infected potato tubers (cull piles or unharvested volunteer potatoes) and in living volunteer tomato plants or solanaceous weeds in protected microclimates.
- Eliminating cull piles, volunteers, and nightshade species within a 1-mile radius of commercial tomato plantings significantly reduces early-season epidemic risk.

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text:
## Cultural Practices & Irrigation Management
1. **Certified Transplants:** Inspect all incoming tomato transplants thoroughly before setting into the field. Reject any flat showing suspicious water-soaked lesions or stem necrosis.
2. **Irrigation Selection:** Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation during periods of cool or cloudy weather. Drip irrigation keeps foliage completely dry, denying the pathogen the 6 to 8 hours of leaf wetness required for spore germination.
3. **Field Layout:** Orient planting rows parallel to prevailing winds to encourage air movement and rapid canopy drying.

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text: 4. **Sanitation:** Disinfect pruning shears, stakes, and implements with bleach or quaternary ammonium compounds between field blocks.

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text:
## Chemical Control & Spray Programs
- Fungicide applications must be initiated before infection occurs. Once late blight is established across more than 5% to 10% of the canopy, chemical control becomes ineffective.
- **Protectant Regimens:** Chlorothalonil (1.5 to 2.1 pt/acre), mancozeb (1.5 to 2.0 lb/acre), or fixed copper applied every 7 to 10 days under low-risk weather, and every 5 days under cool, overcast, rainy conditions.

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text: - **Translaminar / Systemic Regimens:** During active disease pressure, tank-mix protectants with specialized oomycide chemistry such as cymoxanil, dimethomorph (Acrobat), or mandipropamid. Always observe strict label restrictions on maximum applications per season to delay resistance development.

metadata.title: Tomato: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
metadata.institution: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
metadata.authors: R. M. Davis, T. A. Turini

text: # Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 1. Site Selection, Soil Preparation, and pH Balance
Growing healthy, high-yielding tomatoes begins with optimal site selection and soil preparation.
- **Sunlight Requirements:** Tomatoes require full sunlight, needing at least 6 to 8 hours of direct, unobstructed sunlight daily to support vigorous vegetative development and fruit set.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
- **Soil Quality and Drainage:** Tomatoes thrive in well-drained, loose, loamy soil enriched with well-decomposed organic matter or compost (2 to 3 inches incorporated into the top 6 to 8 inches of soil). Heavy, waterlogged clay soils restrict root respiration and encourage root rots and seedling damping-off.
- **Soil pH:** The optimal soil pH for tomato nutrient uptake is between 6.2 and 6.8. If soil testing reveals a pH below 6.0, apply agricultural lime as recommended by a soil test. If pH exceeds 7.2, incorporate elemental sulfur.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 2. Nutrient Management and Balanced Fertilization
Proper fertilization maintains plant vigor without inducing excessive vulnerability to foliar pathogens.
- **Avoid Excessive Nitrogen:** High nitrogen rates stimulate dense, succulent vegetative foliage that impedes air circulation and significantly increases susceptibility to foliar blights and bacterial spot.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
- **Balanced N-P-K Application:** Apply a balanced fertilizer (such as 10-10-10 or 5-10-10) at transplanting according to soil test recommendations. Sidedress with calcium nitrate or balanced fertilizer once the first fruit clusters reach marble size, avoiding direct contact with plant stems.
- **Calcium Availability:** Ensure steady moisture to facilitate calcium uptake, which is essential to prevent blossom-end rot on developing tomato fruit.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 3. Plant Spacing, Staking, and Trellising
Adequate spacing and vertical support are the most effective cultural methods for minimizing foliar disease pressure.
- **Spacing Guidelines:** Space indeterminate tomato plants 24 to 36 inches apart within rows, maintaining 48 to 60 inches between rows. Determinate varieties may be spaced 18 to 24 inches apart. Crowded plantings trap humid microclimates that promote pathogen sporulation.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text: - **Staking and Caging:** Support all tomato plants using wooden or metal stakes, sturdy wire cages, or the Florida weave trellis system. Keeping foliage and fruit elevated off the ground prevents direct soil contact, accelerates leaf drying after rain or dew, and improves spray coverage.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 4. Water Management and Drip Irrigation
Moisture management is critical to tomato vigor and pathogen prevention.
- **Watering Technique:** Always apply water directly to the soil root zone using drip irrigation, soaker hoses, or targeted ground watering. Strictly avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation. Wet foliage provides the free moisture required for bacterial spot, early blight, and late blight spores to germinate and infect.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text: - **Irrigation Timing and Depth:** Irrigate thoroughly and deeply early in the morning (1 to 1.5 inches of water per week, adjusted for natural rainfall). Deep watering encourages extensive, drought-resilient root systems, whereas frequent shallow watering produces weak surface roots.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 5. Mulching and Soil Splash Prevention
- **Mulch Application:** Apply a 2 to 3-inch layer of clean organic mulch (such as clean straw, shredded bark, or untreated wood shavings) or black plastic mulch over the soil around the base of plants after the soil has warmed.
- **Disease Prevention Mechanism:** Mulch conserves soil moisture, moderates soil temperature, suppresses weeds, and crucially acts as a physical barrier that prevents soil-borne fungal spores and bacteria from splashing onto lower leaves during rainfall.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 6. Pruning, Lower Canopy Clearance, and Sanitation
- **Lower Leaf Clearance:** Prune off the lowest 12 to 18 inches of leaves and branches once the plant is established and the first fruit cluster has set. Removing bottom foliage eliminates leaves most susceptible to soil splash and drastically enhances air circulation.
- **Sucker Removal:** For indeterminate varieties, selectively pinch out small axillary suckers to focus plant energy on primary fruit production and keep the plant canopy open.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
- **Sanitation Practices:** Always work in tomato plantings only when foliage is completely dry to prevent mechanical transmission of pathogens. Disinfect pruning shears, stakes, and cages between plants and seasons using a 10% bleach solution or 70% isopropyl alcohol.
- **Rogueing Diseased Tissue:** Immediately remove and destroy heavily diseased lower leaves or severely infected plants. Never compost diseased tomato debris; dispose of it offsite or burn where permitted.

metadata.title: Tomato Cultural Management and General Plant Health Guidelines
metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## 7. Crop Rotation and Seed Selection
- **Rotational Schedule:** Implement a strict 3 to 4-year crop rotation cycle. Never plant tomatoes in soil where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, or eggplants (all members of the Solanaceae family) were cultivated in the preceding three years. Crop rotation starves soil-borne overwintering pathogens.
- **Certified Seed and Transplants:** Always purchase certified disease-free seed or inspect nursery transplants with scrutiny. Select modern cultivars possessing genetic resistance to common foliar diseases whenever available.

metadata.institution: Cornell University Cooperative Extension & Vegetable Program
metadata.authors: Steve Reiners, Abby Seaman, Meg McGrath

text:
## Diagnostic Symptoms of Septoria Leaf Spot

Septoria leaf spot of tomato is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. Symptoms appear primarily on the lower leaves shortly after fruit set. Lesions begin as small, water-soaked circular spots (1.5 to 3.0 mm in diameter). As lesions mature, they develop dark brown margins with distinctive sunken, ash-gray or tan centers. Under 10x magnification, minute black specks (pycnidia - fruiting bodies) are clearly visible embedded in the central gray tissue. Heavily infected leaves turn yellow, chlorotic, wither, and drop prematurely, leading to severe defoliation and sunscald of exposed tomato fruits.

metadata.title: Diagnosis and Integrated Management of Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR Varanasi)
metadata.authors: A. B. Rai, K. K. Pandey, M. Loganathan

text:
## Critical Differential Diagnosis: Septoria Leaf Spot vs Early Blight

Distinguishing Septoria Leaf Spot from Early Blight (Alternaria solani) is critical for accurate agronomic diagnosis. Septoria lesions are characteristically smaller (1.5-3.0 mm), far more numerous per leaflet, and feature distinctive sunken ash-gray centers with tiny black fungal pycnidia embedded inside. In contrast, Early Blight lesions are much larger (5.0-15.0 mm), fewer in number, and display prominent concentric rings (a 'bull's-eye' or target-board pattern) without embedded pycnidia. Furthermore, Early Blight causes dark, sunken leathery cankers on stems and fruit stem-ends, whereas Septoria rarely directly infects the tomato fruit.

metadata.title: Diagnosis and Integrated Management of Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR Varanasi)
metadata.authors: A. B. Rai, K. K. Pandey, M. Loganathan

text:
## Integrated Management and Fungicidal Control of Septoria

Manage Septoria leaf spot through sanitation, 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops, and elimination of horse-nettle and volunteer tomato weeds. Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; employ drip irrigation to maintain dry foliage. Upon first detection of symptoms on lower foliage, apply preventive copper oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L. In high disease pressure under persistent warm rain, spray systemic azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L at 10-14 day intervals, respecting the 5-day pre-harvest interval.

text:
## Symptoms of Tomato Leaf Mold

Tomato leaf mold, caused by Passalora fulva, primarily affects greenhouse, polyhouse, and high-humidity field crops. The earliest visible symptoms appear on the upper surface of older leaves as pale yellow, diffuse chlorotic spots with indefinite borders. On the corresponding lower leaf surface, these spots become covered with a dense, velvety olive-green to grayish-brown fungal mold composed of conidia and conidiophores. As the disease progresses, infected foliage wilts, turns brown, and curls, drying out prematurely.

metadata.title: Identification and Management of Tomato Leaf Mold in Protected Cultivation
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR)

text:
## Environmental Management and Control

Leaf mold requires relative humidity above 85% to sporulate and infect. Primary control is achieved by increasing greenhouse ventilation, spacing plants adequately (60 x 45 cm), maintaining night temperatures to prevent dew formation, and pruning lower foliage to enhance air movement. If fungicidal intervention is required, spray copper hydroxide 53.8% DF @ 2.0 g/L or difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L. Ensure complete spray coverage of lower leaf surfaces where sporulation occurs.

metadata.title: Identification and Management of Tomato Leaf Mold in Protected Cultivation
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR)

text:
## Target Spot Symptomology on Leaves and Fruit

Target spot of tomato is caused by Corynespora casiicola. Foliar symptoms begin as pinpoint water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand into circular to irregular brown spots with pale brown centers and dark brown margins. Unlike Early Blight which exhibits large concentric rings, Target Spot lesions exhibit smaller concentric rings and frequently cause severe upper canopy defoliation. Fruit lesions appear as small, slightly sunken circular specks with dark brown margins that can crack open as the fruit ripens.

metadata.title: Target Spot of Tomato: Symptoms and Chemical Management
metadata.institution: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU Agritech Portal)

text:
## Management Practices for Target Spot

Destroy infected crop residues immediately after harvest. Avoid overhead irrigation and provide adequate plant spacing. For chemical control, apply boscalid + pyraclostrobin (Pristine) or fluopyram + tebuconazole (Luna Experience) @ 1.0 ml/L or mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L at 10-day intervals during periods of high humidity and temperatures between 25-32°C.

metadata.title: Target Spot of Tomato: Symptoms and Chemical Management
metadata.institution: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU Agritech Portal)

text:
## ToMV Foliar and Fruit Symptoms

Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) causes mottled patterns of light and dark green on foliage, leaf curling, blistering, and distortion. In severe strains, leaves become severely narrowed into a stringy or fern-like appearance ('shoestring' symptom). Plants infected early in the season are stunted with reduced fruit set. Infected fruits exhibit uneven ripening, internal brown necrotic streaks in the outer fruit walls (internal browning or vascular necrosis), and significantly reduced market quality.

metadata.title: Epidemiology and Transmission Management of Tomato Mosaic Virus
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI New Delhi)

text:
## Prevention and Decontamination Protocols

ToMV is extremely stable and easily transmitted mechanically via contaminated hands, tools, grafting knives, and pruning shears. It is also seed-borne on the seed coat. Treat seeds with 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) solution for 30 minutes followed by thorough rinsing. Workers must wash hands with soap or 20% non-fat dry milk solution before handling plants. Smokers must wash thoroughly because tobacco products can harbor mosaic viruses. Immediately rogue out and burn infected plants upon first symptom appearance.

metadata.title: Epidemiology and Transmission Management of Tomato Mosaic Virus
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI New Delhi)

text:
## TYLCV Characteristic Symptoms

Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a devastating begomovirus transmitted persistently by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Symptoms include pronounced upward cupping and curling of leaf margins, severe interveinal and marginal chlorosis (yellowing), marked reduction in leaf size, and severely shortened internodes producing a stunted, bushy appearance. When infection occurs prior to flowering, blossom drop is nearly complete, resulting in 100% marketable yield loss.

metadata.title: Vector Management and Resistant Hybrids for Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
metadata.institution: ICAR - National Institute for Plant Biotechnology (NIPB)

text:
## Whitefly Vector Control and Management Strategy

Because TYLCV is whitefly-transmitted, management focuses on vector exclusion. Raise tomato seedlings under 40-mesh insect-proof nylon nets. Install yellow sticky traps (@ 15-20 traps per acre) at canopy height to monitor and mass-trap adult whiteflies. Spray systemic insecticides such as imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 ml/L, thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L, or diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L alternating with 2% neem oil (10,000 ppm) to prevent insecticide resistance. Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., US-440, NS-501, Abhinav) in endemic regions.

metadata.title: Vector Management and Resistant Hybrids for Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
metadata.institution: ICAR - National Institute for Plant Biotechnology (NIPB)

text:
## Spider Mite Damage Symptoms on Tomato Foliage

Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) pierce individual plant cells with stylets and suck sap from leaf undersides. Symptoms begin as minute yellow or white stippling (speckling) on the upper surface of leaves. As populations multiply exponentially during hot, dry weather (temperature >30°C, RH <60%), leaves turn bronze or yellowish-brown, dry up, and drop. Fine silken webbing covers leaf undersides and apical growing points, trapping dust and impairing photosynthesis.

metadata.title: Bio-Intensive and Chemical Management of Spider Mites in Solanaceous Crops
metadata.institution: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR)

text:
## Biological and Acaricidal Management of Spider Mites

Conserve predatory mites (Phytoseiidae such as Neoseiulus longispinosus) and predatory thrips. Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizer application which accelerates mite reproduction. Apply bio-pesticide Beauveria bassiana @ 5 g/L or neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%). When mite density exceeds 5-10 mites per leaflet, spray selective acaricides: propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 ml/L, spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 ml/L, or fenazaquin 10% EC @ 1.5 ml/L. Ensure high-pressure spray reaches the undersides of leaves.

metadata.title: Bio-Intensive and Chemical Management of Spider Mites in Solanaceous Crops
metadata.institution: ICAR - National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources (NBAIR)

text:
## Wheat Rust Diseases: Yellow (Stripe) and Brown (Leaf) Rust

Stripe rust (Yellow rust) caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici is the foremost threat in Northern Plains and hill zones. It forms yellow pustules (uredinia) arranged in distinct linear stripes along leaf veins. Leaf rust (Brown rust) caused by Puccinia triticina produces small, round to oval orange-brown pustules scattered randomly over leaf blades without forming stripes. Rust spores are wind-borne; cool temperatures (10-15°C) with fog favor yellow rust, while warmer temperatures (15-25°C) favor brown rust.

metadata.title: Comprehensive Wheat Production Technology and Rust Management in India
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Wheat and Barley Research (IIWBR Karnal)
metadata.authors: Gyanendra Singh, Sendhil R., O. P. Gangwar

text:
## Critical Irrigation Stages for Wheat

Wheat requires 4 to 6 irrigations at physiological critical growth stages: 1. Crown Root Initiation (CRI at 20-25 days after sowing - most critical; moisture stress here cuts yield by 30%), 2. Tillering stage (40-45 DAS), 3. Late Jointing stage (60-65 DAS), 4. Flowering stage (80-85 DAS), 5. Milk stage (100-105 DAS), and 6. Dough stage (115-120 DAS). Avoid irrigation during high winds at grain-filling to prevent lodging.

metadata.title: Comprehensive Wheat Production Technology and Rust Management in India
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Wheat and Barley Research (IIWBR Karnal)
metadata.authors: Gyanendra Singh, Sendhil R., O. P. Gangwar

text:
## Nutrient Management and High-Yielding Wheat Varieties

Recommended fertilizer dose for timely-sown irrigated wheat is 120-150 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 40 kg K2O per hectare. Apply all P, K, and 1/3 N as basal dose at sowing; top-dress remaining N in two equal splits after first and second irrigations. In zinc-deficient soils, apply 25 kg zinc sulfate (21% Zn) per hectare. High-yielding rust-resistant varieties include DBW-187 (Karan Vandana), DBW-303 (Karan Vaishnavi), HD-2967, HD-3086, and PBW-725.

metadata.title: Comprehensive Wheat Production Technology and Rust Management in India
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Wheat and Barley Research (IIWBR Karnal)
metadata.authors: Gyanendra Singh, Sendhil R., O. P. Gangwar

text:
## Chemical Control of Stripe Rust in Wheat

Upon detecting the first foci of yellow rust in the field, immediately spray propiconazole 25% EC (Tilt) @ 1.0 ml/L or tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L in 200 liters of water per acre. A single well-timed spray at initial incidence halts rust progression and protects the flag leaf which contributes over 50% of grain dry matter.

text:
## Rice Blast: Leaf Blast and Neck Blast Identification

Rice blast, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia oryzae), attacks all aerial parts. Leaf blast lesions are spindle-shaped (eye-shaped) with grey or whitish centers and brown or reddish-brown borders. Neck blast occurs when the fungus infects the panicle base (neck node), causing the neck to turn blackish-brown and rot, resulting in sterile empty grains ('whiteheads') or panicle breakage.

metadata.institution: ICAR - National Rice Research Institute (NRRI Cuttack)
metadata.authors: P. C. Rath, S. D. Mohapatra, B. C. Patra

text:
## Bacterial Blight and Sheath Blight of Rice

Bacterial leaf blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae) produces wavy, water-soaked marginal lesions on leaf blades that turn yellow to straw-colored, with milky bacterial ooze droplets visible early morning. Sheath blight (Rhizoctonia solani) produces large, greenish-grey oval lesions on leaf sheaths near water level that coalesce into irregular snake-skin patterns, causing lodging.

metadata.title: Package of Practices for High-Yielding Paddy and Major Disease Management
metadata.institution: ICAR - National Rice Research Institute (NRRI Cuttack)
metadata.authors: P. C. Rath, S. D. Mohapatra, B. C. Patra

text:
## Nutrient Management and Cultivation Techniques in Rice

Apply recommended NPK @ 100-120:50-60:40-50 kg/ha. Apply full P2O5 and 50% K2O as basal; split nitrogen into three applications: 50% at basal/active tillering, 25% at panicle initiation, and 25% at boot leaf stage. In Direct Seeded Rice (DSR), maintain weed-free condition during first 30 days using pre-emergence pendimethalin 30% EC @ 1.0 kg a.i./ha followed by post-emergence bispyribac-sodium 10% SC @ 25 g a.i./ha at 15-20 DAS. For blast control, spray tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 ml/L.

text:
## Fall Armyworm Identification and Crop Damage Symptoms

Fall Armyworm (FAW - Spodoptera frugiperda) is an aggressive invasive pest attacking maize from seedling to cob harvest. Early instar larvae scrape green leaf tissue causing characteristic 'papery windows' on leaves. Older larvae migrate into the central whorl, feeding voraciously and producing prominent ragged pinholes, extensive leaf shredding, and large quantities of coarse, sawdust-like brownish frass inside the whorl. Larvae feature four dark spots forming a square on the 8th abdominal segment and an inverted 'Y' suture on the dark head capsule.

metadata.title: Maize Cultivation Guide and Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) IPM
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Maize Research (IIMR Ludhiana)
metadata.authors: Sujay Rakshit, J. C. Sekhar, Pradyumn Kumar

text:
## Integrated Pest Management (IPM) for Fall Armyworm

Implement IPM from sowing: Deep summer plowing exposes pupae to predators. Install pheromone traps (@ 5 traps/acre) immediately after germination to monitor adult moth flights. Conserve natural enemies (egg parasitoids Telenomus remus, Trichogramma). Apply 5% neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) or azadirachtin 10,000 ppm @ 2 ml/L at early vegetative stage. If whorl damage exceeds 10%, apply targeted whorl sprays of chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC @ 0.4 ml/L or emamectin benzoate 5% SG @ 0.4 g/L using a nozzle directed straight into the plant whorls.

text:
## Soil Testing Protocol and Soil Health Card Interpretation

Collect representative soil samples following a zigzag pattern across the field at 0-15 cm depth for field crops and 0-30 cm for horticultural crops. Test for 12 key parameters: pH, Electrical Conductivity (EC), Organic Carbon (OC), available Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P2O5), Potassium (K2O), Sulfur (S), and micronutrients Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), Copper (Cu), Manganese (Mn), and Boron (B). Optimal soil pH is 6.5 to 7.5; organic carbon should ideally exceed 0.75%. Electrical conductivity below 1.0 dS/m indicates non-saline soil.

metadata.title: Soil Health Management, Soil Testing and Balanced Nutrient Application
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Soil Science (IISS Bhopal)

text:
## Correction of Acidic and Saline/Alkaline Soils

In acidic soils (pH < 6.0), phosphorus fixation occurs, reducing availability. Correct by applying agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) or dolomite @ 2 to 4 tonnes/ha based on buffer pH test every 3 years. In sodic/alkaline soils (pH > 8.5 with high exchangeable sodium), apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) calculated from gypsum requirement (GR), followed by leaching with good quality irrigation water. Incorporate green manuring crops like Dhaincha (Sesbania aculeata) to lower soil pH naturally through organic acids.

metadata.title: Soil Health Management, Soil Testing and Balanced Nutrient Application
metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Soil Science (IISS Bhopal)

text:
## Organic Carbon Enrichment and Biofertilizers

Maintain soil microbiological health by applying 10 tonnes of well-rotted Farmyard Manure (FYM) or 3-5 tonnes of vermicompost per hectare annually. Inoculate seeds or soil with Rhizobium (for pulses), Azotobacter or Azospirillum (for cereals), and Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) @ 10 g/kg seed or 2.5 kg/ha in 50 kg FYM. PSB solubilizes fixed insoluble tricalcium phosphate into bioavailable monocalcium form, improving P fertilizer efficiency by 20-30%.

metadata.institution: ICAR - Indian Institute of Soil Science (IISS Bhopal)

text:
## Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN)

PM-KISAN is a central sector scheme providing direct income support of ₹6,000 per year to all landholding farmer families across India. The financial benefit is transferred directly into beneficiaries' Aadhaar-linked bank accounts in three equal installments of ₹2,000 every four months. Farmers must complete e-KYC on the pmkisan.gov.in portal or via biometric verification at Common Service Centers (CSCs). Land records must be seeded in the state portal for verification.

metadata.title: Government Agricultural Support Schemes: PM-KISAN, PMFBY, Soil Health Card and KCC
metadata.institution: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India

text:
## Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY)

PMFBY provides comprehensive crop insurance cover against non-preventable natural risks (drought, flood, unseasonal rain, hailstorm, pests, and diseases). Farmer premium rates are capped at 2.0% of sum insured for Kharif food and oilseed crops, 1.5% for Rabi crops, and 5.0% for commercial and annual horticultural crops. The remaining actuarial premium is subsidized equally by Central and State Governments. Post-harvest localized losses must be reported within 72 hours via the Crop Insurance App or toll-free number 14447.

metadata.title: Government Agricultural Support Schemes: PM-KISAN, PMFBY, Soil Health Card and KCC
metadata.institution: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Government of India

text:
## Kisan Credit Card (KCC) and Subsidized Institutional Credit

The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme provides farmers with flexible, timely institutional short-term credit for crop cultivation, post-harvest expenses, and farm maintenance. Baseline interest rate is 9.0%, with a 2.0% interest subvention by the Central Government, lowering the rate to 7.0%. An additional 3.0% Prompt Repayment Incentive (PRI) reduces the effective interest rate to only 4.0% per annum for loans up to ₹3 lakh. Collateral-free agricultural loans are sanctioned up to ₹1.60 lakh.
